content:
Cells going through meiosis must divide twice because meiosis has **two different jobs** to accomplish:

1) **Reduce the chromosome number from diploid (2n) to haploid (n)**  
- In **Meiosis I**, homologous chromosome pairs (one set from each parent) are separated into different cells.  
- This is the *reduction division*: one cell with 2n chromosomes becomes **two cells with n chromosomes** (still with duplicated chromosomes—each chromosome is made of two sister chromatids).

2) **Separate the duplicated DNA (sister chromatids) without changing chromosome number again**  
- Before meiosis starts, DNA is copied once in S phase, so each chromosome has two sister chromatids.  
- In **Meiosis II**, sister chromatids are separated, similar to mitosis.  
- This produces **four haploid cells**, each with single (unduplicated) chromosomes.

Key idea: **DNA replicates once, but cells divide twice.**  
If there were only one division after DNA replication, the products would still have chromosomes made of two chromatids and would not produce the typical four genetically distinct haploid gametes needed for sexual reproduction.
